html:
The Tuareg are a Berber people of the central Sahara, traditionally nomadic herders of camels and goats, in what is now southern Algeria, southwestern Libya, Niger and Mali. On this map they are shown in 900.

Their ancestors were Berber groups pushed or drawn south into the desert, perhaps as Arab armies spread through North Africa. In the Saharan massifs of Ahaggar and Aïr they kept their own language, Tamasheq, and their own script, Tifinagh, descended from ancient Libyan writing. Tuareg men, not women, wear the veil, and family descent and property often pass through the mother.

Living on the routes between North Africa and the Sahel, the Tuareg guided, taxed, protected and raided the caravans of the trans-Saharan trade, which carried salt, gold, cloth and slaves. Later they took part in the life of desert towns such as Agadez and Timbuktu. See also the map's later label, Touareg.
